title: The Zócalo International Book Fair Ended; Nearly 2 Million People Attended, Paloma Saiz Says
author: Reyes Martínez Torrijos
content:
_This article by[Reyes Martínez
Torrijos](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Reyes%20Mart%C3%ADnez%20Torrijos)
originally appeared in the [October 19, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/10/19/cultura/termino-la-fil-
del-zocalo-asistieron-casi-2-millones-de-personas-paloma-saiz), Mexico's
premier left wing daily newspaper._

After 10 days of reflection, artistic expressions, book presentations and
solidarity, the 26th edition of the Zócalo International Book Fair concluded
this Sunday. Its director, Paloma Saiz, commented that this year is “when I’ve
seen the most people.” She estimated that more than one and a half million
people attended.

The cultural promoter said that the forums are full of audiences and “the
bookstores are selling much more, like never before. It means we are winning:
**people are reading**.”

She noted that during the covid pandemic capacity was reduced, and some
800,000 people were registered. “Now it is calculated that **more than one and
a half million, almost 2 million** ” attended this edition.

“The fact that makes me very happy is that the exhibitors report that ‘they
are selling like they never had before,’” she stated.

The afternoon in the Zócalo, under a Sun that at moments has summer vestiges,
was the center of a diverse attitude. There were children already reading the
books that had been bought for them. A young woman firmly states that her idea
is to go “take a walk around” the fair, in response to the question of the
woman who appears to be her mother.

Among the stands a multitude of conversations take place about books, prices,
social phenomena. There are people who cross the aisles already with their
copies open and show them off to their companions; there are those who eat a
snack, or the girl who walks along, focused, reading the back cover of a book
by Charles Bukowski.

In the middle of the capital’s plaza and amid a crowd of people in search of
books and conversations, Saiz highlighted: “I see **many more young people**
than I normally used to see.”

She added that “a long time ago we had an audience of people in their forties
and up. Now I have seen a great number of young people. We have a comics
pavilion that has attracted them a lot, but in addition the program is
designed for everyone. It has many things they like.”

> Greater awareness is beginning to emerge among them about the moments we are
> living. That is why activities like these are essential, where they listen
> to intelligent people, not fake news; here they hear talks by people who
> know what they are saying.
>
> Paloma Saiz

Paloma Saiz reported that the Zócalo FIL gave away five books, which were
added to another five provided by the Brigada para Leer en Libertad. It
reached a figure of some **40,000 copies given away** in these 10 days.

The aisles reveal the delight seen in the visitors. In their attentive gaze as
they tour the tents there is desire, interest in the worlds contained in the
writings.

The gathering’s four forums appear packed for a good part of the more than 40
activities this Sunday. In one of them a talk led by journalist Julio
Hernández ends and a conversation begins with Argentine novelist Dolores
Reyes, who last year suffered harassment in her country.

The author of _Cometierra_ says that left-wing governments have a greater
number of female voters and those of the ultra-right are fed by a majority of
male voters. She thus sketches a brief picture of feminism in Argentina and
Mexico.

Meanwhile, writer Liliana Escliar said in that space that there have been
advances in favor of women, but there are threats due to the growth of
conservative governments in the region.

In another forum, Paco Ignacio Taibo II talks about _Los esbirros del palacio_
, by illustrator Augusto Mora. Further on, novelist Juan Villoro talks about
soccer and stresses that the refusal of the promotion mechanism in the Mexican
soccer league is an attack on democracy. He refers to Uruguayan writer Eduardo
Galeano, who believed that people should not be prevented from enjoying this
sport.

The general atmosphere is one of reflection, of interest in books or the
current situation of Mexico and the rest of the world. At times, decades of
history are addressed to establish intellectual scenarios, or emotion is
expressed through music, as in the recital by singer Leiden, granddaughter of
Cuban poet Roberto Fernández Retamar.

Interest is present. There are people on bicycles, in wheelchairs, with
strollers and on foot. A teenager excitedly asks her parents to accompany her
to a stand. Two young people cross with the _One Piece_ flag held high. The
day begins to cloud over and the final night of the Zócalo FIL 2026 arrives.
